extracted.intended_audience: mathematics education researchers and undergraduate calculus instructors
extracted.subtask_description: Framework and empirical criteria for observing and interpreting undergraduate students' understanding of the limit concept (via interviews, tasks, modalities, and justification). Useful for researchers designing studies or instructors creating assessments to probe limit understanding.

rubrics_metrics.name: Three-strand model: Method, Justification, Applicability
rubrics_metrics.description: Student understanding of the limit concept is seen through three interconnected strands: method (how they approach problems), justification (how they explain/validate their work), and applicability (whether method and justification tie to the problem context).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The strands should be observed together; a missing or broken link among them can indicate a gap in understanding. Visual representations (Figure 5) depict justification and method as boxes with applicability connecting them to the limit concept.

rubrics_metrics.name: Method: Four modalites (Symbolic, Visual, Verbal, Numeric)
rubrics_metrics.description: Students' chosen methods fall into four main modalities: (1) Symbolic, (2) Visual, (3) Verbal, and (4) Numeric.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When observing student work, classify behaviors, recorded symbols, and words into these modalities to understand their perspective on limits. Different tasks can elicit different modalities; modality choice itself is diagnostic.

rubrics_metrics.name: Symbolic modality
rubrics_metrics.description: Denoted by creation of algebraic examples, algebraic procedures/rules learned in class (e.g., applying l'Hôpital's rule), and generation of symbolic records.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Includes use of formal definitions when context requires it. Examples: Amos creating algebraic functions, Bud using l'Hôpital's rule for Task 6a. Symbolic often aligns with syntactic justification but can include formal-definition subcomponents.

rubrics_metrics.name: Visual modality
rubrics_metrics.description: Use of graphs and visual aids to evaluate limits or reason about families of functions (generic graphical representations).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Look for students drawing graphs or reasoning about local behavior around the point of interest (e.g., Arlene and Barry). Visual methods can be used to both generate examples and to verify algebraic work.

rubrics_metrics.name: Verbal modality
rubrics_metrics.description: Talking through a solution without making a symbolic record; may include analogies, metaphors, or gestural/perceptuomotor behavior.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because audio-only data may obscure subcategories, researchers should consider additional data collection (video) to capture gestures/other perceptuomotor evidence. Verbal reasoning can translate to other modalities or serve as its own line of thought.

rubrics_metrics.name: Numeric modality
rubrics_metrics.description: Creating tables of values or plugging in numbers near the point of interest to approximate or verify limits.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Often used as a secondary or verification method (e.g., Arlene using values close to 2). Numeric approaches may be underused in formal assessments but are diagnostic of students' informal sense-making.

rubrics_metrics.name: Justification types: Syntactic vs Semantic
rubrics_metrics.description: Justification breaks into two main components: syntactic (staying within the framework or representation of the question, e.g., algebraic manipulations) and semantic (translating the problem into another representation or interpretation).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Syntactic example: applying algebraic procedures because the problem was presented algebraically. Semantic example: graphing or numerically testing to interpret meaning. Judges of understanding should assess both the type and correctness/applicability of the justification.

rubrics_metrics.name: Correctness and applicability of justification
rubrics_metrics.description: Beyond type, the justification must be correct and applicable to the limit in question; merely executing procedures without understanding why is limited value.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether the justification validates the method and whether the student recognizes when a method or justification does not apply. Failures of applicability signal target points for instruction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Applicability (the connecting strand)
rubrics_metrics.description: Applicability ties method and justification to each other and to the specific limit concept: can the selected method lead to a solution, does the justification validate the method, and does the student recognize applicability in context?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use applicability as a diagnostic: if any link fails, it indicates a gap in understanding. Encourage students to identify inapplicability themselves when possible; such metacognitive recognition makes remediation easier.

rubrics_metrics.name: Flexibility across modalities as indicator of stronger understanding
rubrics_metrics.description: Students who demonstrate facility and flexibility switching between modalities may possess a stronger understanding of limits than students who are 'stuck' in a single modality.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating students, note whether they can re-express solutions in another modality (e.g., symbolic→visual→numeric) and whether they use multiple modalities to verify answers. Lack of switching can indicate limited conceptual connections.

rubrics_metrics.name: Formal-definition use as a subcomponent of symbolic modality
rubrics_metrics.description: Use of the formal epsilon-delta definition is likely to occur with symbolic methods and is categorized under syntactic justification when it arises in the correct context.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because formal-definition reasoning may only emerge in contexts that require it, include tasks that prompt formal reasoning if assessing that component specifically. The dashed lines in the model indicate where formal-definition links are most likely.

rubrics_metrics.name: Perceptuomotor behaviors (gestures) within verbal modality
rubrics_metrics.description: Gestures and other perceptuomotor actions are hypothesized subcomponents of the verbal modality and may reveal additional insight into student reasoning.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Current audio-only data are insufficient; researchers should collect video data to classify and interpret perceptuomotor evidence. Consider these behaviors when assessing students' non-symbolic sense-making.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assessment design: require verification using another method
rubrics_metrics.description: When designing exams or formative assessments, include questions that require both finding an answer and verifying it using another method/modal representation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This pedagogical design elicits and rewards cross-modal connections and helps reveal whether students can translate between methods (improves diagnosis of conceptual understanding).

rubrics_metrics.name: Sociomathematical norm components (expectation, negotiation, normative)
rubrics_metrics.description: A sociomathematical norm is characterized by three components: (1) a mathematical expectation is set forth, (2) the expectation is negotiated by participants, and (3) the expectation becomes normative.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use this tripartite structure to identify and study norms in classroom interactions, especially in inquiry-based settings. These components are not necessarily hierarchical or chronological.

rubrics_metrics.name: Negotiation subcomponents for sociomathematical norms
rubrics_metrics.description: Within negotiation, three subcomponents should be identified: (a) a mathematical interpretation of the expectation occurs, (b) the expectation is agreed upon, and (c) the expectation is validated as legitimate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Pay particular attention to validation as legitimacy; without perceived legitimacy participants may reject a proposed norm even if it has been introduced by authority.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sociomathematical event and quasi sociomathematical norm
rubrics_metrics.description: A 'sociomathematical event' is any event containing a component of a sociomathematical norm; a 'quasi sociomathematical norm' is a group of events that have some but not all components of a full norm (e.g., introduced and negotiated but not yet normative).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These terms help researchers focus on developmental stages of norms in classroom discourse without requiring the norm to have fully stabilized.

rubrics_metrics.name: Authority relation components (authority relation, legitimacy, change)
rubrics_metrics.description: Authority in classrooms hinges on three major concepts: authority relation (bearer and receiver), legitimacy (knowledge/skills/position/experience that influence receivers), and change (the receiver being influenced to change thinking/behavior).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When analyzing classroom interactions, identify who acts as bearer/receiver, what legitimizes that bearer, and whether the interaction leads to change in students' thinking or behavior.

rubrics_metrics.name: Types of authority (hierarchal, mathematical, expertise, performative)
rubrics_metrics.description: Four types of authority legitimize claims in classroom interactions: (1) hierarchal authority (position-based), (2) mathematical authority (based in mathematics), (3) expertise authority (based on expertise), and (4) performative authority (based on ability to engage the class).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Different authorities play different roles in norm introduction and negotiation. The paper notes hierarchal and mathematical authority were especially salient in their data; consider all four when interpreting who legitimizes norms.
